title: 3,600 automated matches say my game is balanced. Why does it still feel unfair?
author: Carlox979
selftext:
I’m developing V-FORGE: Rune Hunt, a turn-based hex strategy game prototype, with the help of AI coding tools.  
During manual playtesting, I noticed something strange: playing as Forge against the Void AI felt consistently unfair. Void seemed to reach the central Rune more easily, even though both factions had symmetrical starting positions and paths on a 51-hex battlefield.  
Instead of immediately changing the game balance, I used AI-assisted development to investigate.  
With AI coding assistance, I worked on checking the hex-grid geometry, mirrored starting positions, obstacles and objective distances. I also used automated match simulations to compare outcomes.  
In version 0.5.1, I ran 3,600 simulated matches:  
Forge wins: 1,774  
Void wins: 1,786  
Draws: 40  
Statistically, the results were almost perfectly balanced.  
But when actually playing, Forge still felt disadvantaged.  
That’s the interesting problem I’m facing: **a game can produce balanced results without necessarily feeling fair to the player.**  
I’m now investigating opening moves, movement decisions, initiative and how clearly the available routes are communicated.  
The issue isn’t resolved yet, and I’m trying not to confuse automated test results with actual player experience.  
For developers who use AI coding assistants:  
**How would you test the gap between statistical balance and perceived fairness?**  
Would you focus on turn-by-turn movement logs, mirrored opening sequences, first-arrival times at objectives, or human playtesting?  
I’d really appreciate practical feedback from anyone who has encountered something similar.

comments.author: caesium23
comments.body:
There are a couple important points here. 

1. As other comments have already pointed out, no computer is going to play the same way a human does. I use bots as part of playtesting a game I'm working on, and even after adding some minimal reaction time delays, they still play with the speed and focus of a machine. I can't play fast enough to even come close to keeping up with them on scoring.

2. Single player games aren't meant to be fair or balanced. Any ordinary single player game is actually designed to be heavily unbalanced _in the player's favor_. Think about how unbalanced a fight between Mario and a goomba is -- and it has to be, because in a legitimately fair fight you would lose to the first goomba 50% of the time (talk about a short game). I'm sure there are exceptions to this (maybe soulslikes), but it is the norm, and if you play many single player games it's going to influence your sense of what you expect "fair and balanced" to feel like.

This is so pervasive that it actually makes balancing multiplayer games problematic. If each side wins 50% of the time (as they will in a perfectly fair and balanced game), each side ends up convinced that the other side has an unfair advantage. I believe something similar to the Dunning-Kruger effect is involved here: everyone believes they're "good" at the game, so in a "fair" game they should be able to win more often than not. If the other side wins as often as they do, that can't be because the other side is just as good as them -- the game must be unfair.

replies.author: Carlox979
replies.body:
That’s a really interesting distinction between statistical balance and what feels fair in a single-player game.  
Right now I’m testing Rune Hunt against the Void AI, and I’m starting to realize that a 50/50 result in automated simulations doesn’t necessarily translate into a satisfying human experience.  
I want to keep the underlying rules consistent, but make the early decisions feel understandable and meaningful.  
In your experience, would you first adjust the AI’s opening behavior, or improve how the available choices are communicated to the player?

comments.author: Carlox979
comments.body:
That’s a good point. I’m beginning to think I should focus less on tiny statistical differences and more on whether the player understands why they’re winning or losing.  
Have you ever solved a balancing problem by improving feedback or presentation rather than changing the actual game rules?

comments.author: Skubcraft
comments.body:
I'm got more of an RPG thing going on in my project. So my limitations on the Player Bots come down to stress testing to see how far brute force strategies can go. Can all the party variations just slam attack and still get through? Can they get through without items, can the bare minimum beat bosses. That kind of thing. Once an absolute baseline is set, then I go in manually and start manually playtesting and iterating. 

My goal is really to test basic functionality and build from there the interesting and fun stuff while at the iterative design stage. Balance should never be the goal because the machine just can't do it unless you specialize.

comments.author: Ok-Ninja-8165
comments.body: Game feel and balance aren't the same thing. Game can be perfectly balanced and be unfun. And AI can't help you there.
